gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-23.jpg
gallery.description:
Standing Tara. Outer entrance, south wall of Monastery 1, Ratnagiri

This niche sculpture is located to the right of the outer
entrance. The daughter of Avalokiteshvara is accompanied by flying celestials (top) and ascetics carrying water pots (middle). Her right hand extends in varada mudra, the gesture of giving.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-40.jpg
gallery.description:
Seated Tara. Detail from a Bodhisattva statue. West of inner entrance of Monastery 1, Ratnagiri

This lovely Tara is a companion to the headless statue of Avalokiteshvara on site. Tara extends her right hand in
varada mudra, while a lotus flower curls above her left shoulder.
The features of the small statue seem typically
Southeast Asian; as a center of learning, Ratnagiri was visited
by Buddhist travelers from that region, and there were political and trading ties between Orissa and SE Asia
at this time.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-32.jpg
gallery.description: Kubera was adopted into Buddhism as Panchika, representing the wealth of enlightenment. While (as usual in India's additive culture) all possible meanings really apply at once, in this case the overall symbolism of "prosperity" seems to predominate over any specifically Buddhist understandings of these figures.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-47.jpg
gallery.description:
Monks' Cells. Inner wall of Monastery 1, Ratnagiri
This reconstructed section of the west inner wall shows that it
was fashioned like a row of shrines, into which the
monks' cells were set.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-73.jpg
gallery.description:
Seated Buddha, 11th century. Ratnagiri Museum
The Buddha sits in bhumisparsha mudra beneath a stylized Pipal tree (above his halo). Decorations include flying celestials, birds with elaborate tails, gajasimhas with riders, lions, and
worshipers along the base.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-61.jpg
gallery.description:
Head of Buddha. Monastery 1, Ratnagiri
This imposing head of Buddha is displayed
along the edge of the monastery courtyard. The
prominent bulge of its eyes, hidden behind downcast
eyelids, seems to hint at the Buddha's contemplation
of inner mysteries.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-39.jpg
gallery.description:
Acrobatic Figures. Inner entrance of Monastery 1, Ratnagiri
A lively acrobatic figure is climbing the foliage, while the one at left is humorously "mooning" the viewer.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-25.jpg
gallery.description:
Vajrapani. East of inner entrance, Monastery 1 of Ratnagiri
The bodhisattva is identified as Vajrapani by the shapes
of his crown and lotus flower. His upper right hand grasps a rosary, while the lower right hand displays varada mudra in front of an open lotus. His lower left holds the handle of a chauri, again presented on a lotus. Above the bodhisattva are two meditating Buddhas on lotus thrones; at his feet are two kneelng figures.
Ratnagiri belonged to the Vajrayana (esoteric) school of Mahayana Buddhism. Its art is also connected to Java, due to marriage ties between their rulers.
An example is the four-armed "Indonesian style" figure by the bodhisattva's left foot.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-28.jpg
gallery.description:
Avalokiteshvara. West of inner entrance. Monastery 1, Ratnagiri

Sitting at the Bodhisattva's feet are his usual companions, Tara
and Brikuti, each with four arms. The standing attendant is probably Hayagriva, a fierce form of the
Bodhisattva, although his typical horse-shaped hair ornament is
missing here.

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-26.jpg

gallery.title: File:Ratnagiri ei3-36.jpg
gallery.description:
Kubera is a yaksha (nature-spirit), the guardian of buried
treasure, as indicated by
the pots beneath his throne.
He was adopted into Buddhism as Panchika, representing the wealth of enlightenment.
While (as usual in India's additive culture) all possible meanings
really apply at once, in this case the overall symbolism
of "prosperity" seems to predominate over any specifically Buddhist

understandings of these figures.
